subtopics.title: Distribution and Density — Two Different Ideas

questions.question: Population density is best defined as:
options: The pattern of where people are spread across an area
The total number of people living in a country
The average number of people per unit of area, usually per square kilometre
The number of people moving into an area each year

questions.question: Two wards each cover 1 200 km² and each hold 72 000 people, but in one the people live on scattered smallholdings while in the other they all live in a single fishing town. This proves that:
options: Areas with the same density can have completely different distributions
The clustered ward must have the higher density
Distribution can only be measured as a number
The scattered ward has no measurable density

questions.question: Settlement that bunches around a single point is described as:
options: Linear
Clustered or nucleated
Dispersed
Sparse

questions.question: An area described as UNINHABITED is one where:
options: Few people are spread over a large area
People live only along rivers
Population is falling
Nobody lives at all, as on ice caps and the harshest deserts

subtopics.title: Calculating Density — and What It Hides

questions.question: A district holds 189 000 people on 1 400 km². Its population density is:
options: 1 350 people per km²
13,5 people per km²
135 people per km²
189 people per km²

questions.question: KwaZulu-Natal has a density of around 130 people per km² while the Northern Cape has under 4, yet the national average is just over 50. This shows that a national density figure:
options: Is always calculated incorrectly
Is an average that conceals enormous internal contrasts and describes no real place
Applies accurately to every province
Cannot be compared between provinces

questions.question: Writing a density answer as "135" with no unit is a problem because:
options: Density has no unit
The unit is always people per hectare
The number should be rounded to 100 first
A density is meaningless without its unit, people per square kilometre

questions.question: Dividing population by ARABLE land instead of total land is useful because it shows:
options: How many people each unit of productive farmland must support
The exact location of every farm
A country's total mineral wealth
How fast the population is growing

questions.question: The single most powerful physical influence on where people live is:
options: The direction of prevailing winds
Distance from the sea
Climate — moderate temperatures with reliable rainfall
The age of the underlying rock

questions.question: The high interior of Lesotho and the Drakensberg escarpment carry few people mainly because:
options: They receive no rainfall at all
Steep broken terrain means thin soils, hard access and costly building
The law forbids settlement there
They have no minerals

questions.question: The volcanic soils of Java and the delta silts of Bangladesh support some of the world's densest rural populations because:
options: They are close to large cities
They contain valuable minerals
They have very cold winters
Deep fertile soil feeds many people from each hectare of farmland

questions.question: Mining can plant dense settlement in otherwise repellent places because:
options: A mineral deposit is fixed in the earth, so people must move to it
Mines create fertile soil
Miners prefer harsh climates
Minerals are always found near rivers

subtopics.title: Human Factors and South Africa's Pattern

questions.question: The broad east-west contrast in South Africa's population is mainly caused by:
options: Rainfall, which declines westward below roughly 500 mm a year
Better roads in the east
Colder temperatures in the west
The location of the national capital

questions.question: Gauteng holds about a quarter of South Africa's people on under 2% of its land because:
options: It has the country's best harbour
It has the country's most fertile farmland
Witwatersrand gold drew workers, industry and finance, and the concentration outlived the gold
It has an unusually mild coastal climate

questions.question: Very high rural densities in former homeland areas such as QwaQwa, Venda and Gazankulu are best explained by:
options: Exceptional soil fertility in those areas
Apartheid legislation that compressed the majority of the population onto a fraction of the land
Their position on major trade routes
Unusually high rainfall totals

questions.question: The recommended order for a written answer about a population pattern is:
options: Explanation first, then the pattern
Evidence only, with no pattern statement
A list of factors in alphabetical order
State the pattern, point to the evidence, then explain it

questions.question: Moving sixty passengers from a packed bus onto a long open beach changes:
options: The number of people
The density, because the same people now occupy far more space
The birth rate
Nothing at all

questions.question: Calling all sixty people from along the waterline to crowd around the tidal pool changes:
options: The distribution but not the density
The density but not the distribution
Both the density and the distribution
Neither the density nor the distribution

questions.question: A question that asks for DENSITY should be answered with:
options: A word-picture of the pattern
A description of migration routes
A list of physical factors
A number with its unit — people per square kilometre

questions.question: In the dry Richtersveld, settlement clings to the Orange River in a thin line because:
options: The river marks a political boundary
Water is the first requirement for settlement, so people string along the only source
The riverbanks are the flattest land in the region
Roads can only be built beside rivers

questions.question: Kathu exists in the middle of the dry Northern Cape because:
options: It has unusually high rainfall
It lies on a natural harbour
Iron ore lies beneath it, and ore cannot be moved to the people
Its soils are exceptionally fertile

questions.question: Saldanha grew into a port town on a quiet stretch of west coast because:
options: A deep natural harbour gathers trade, and people gather on trade
It receives the most rain on the west coast
It sits on a gold reef
Its beaches attract holidaymakers

questions.question: Comparing South Africa's rainfall map with its population map shows that:
options: People avoid areas of high rainfall
Population is spread evenly regardless of rain
Most people live along the dry west coast
People follow the rain — the wetter east holds most of the population

questions.question: The growth chain that built Gauteng ran:
options: Gold discovery, miners, towns and services, engineering works, banks and offices, railways
Harbour, fishing, farming, tourism
Fertile soil, farms, market towns, cities
Government offices, schools, factories, mines

questions.question: Gauteng keeps its huge population even though the gold reef is largely mined out because:
options: New gold is still being discovered there every year
Jobs, roads and people, once gathered, hold one another in place
The government pays people to stay
The climate is the best in the country

questions.question: Richards Bay grew from a quiet lagoon into an industrial city after the 1970s because:
options: A gold reef was discovered beneath the lagoon
Its farmland is the best in KwaZulu-Natal
A deep harbour was built, drawing coal exports, smelters and then a city
The homelands were located nearby

questions.question: The lesson's three-point summary of South Africa's population map is:
options: Even spread; no large cities; coastal settlement only
Dense west and empty east; two city clusters; no rural crowding
All settlement follows railways; rain is irrelevant; history is irrelevant
Full east and empty west from rain; four city clusters from gold and harbours; crowded rural pockets from history
